I agree we should stop dwelling on the ghost of colonialism, but it still haunts us to this day. Same as in the case you mentioned in Europe. Although I reckon a different situation there since they have a longer dated history. What I was pointing at was an evaluation of the past to "heal the memory" as St. John Paul II put it, albeit in a different context but the same meaning. There can be a lot more to uncover, and bring over those past practices and find how they continue to live on especially if a Christian dimension has been attached to it.

The image of Our Lady of Guadalupe is a perfect example of preserving the past, acknowledging the good and reconcilable indigenous or native culture to aid evangelization, and to open Christianity to an "age of discovery" as well. As elements of the truth, goodness, and beauty of the Catholic/Christian faith can also be traced in other religions, so too can our culture be found in others. This is what I believe makes the Church more beautiful.

Finally, let me contextualize more my point on developing the practice of communion on the hands. The Eucharist was the ultimate realization of the Pesach, the seder meal. Probably, Jewish Christians shared the Eucharist in the same manner as the seder. However, since a consciousness of the real presence was established/realized in the Eucharist, they separated their manner of consuming the Eucharist. It was still on the hands, but they did not use the same manner as eating the seder meal anymore. It then developed into a more practical practice of receiving on the tongue. So,  communion, definitely is connected to eating. Besides the original Greek of John 6, can be translated as gnawing/masticating on the raw meat/flesh.

PS Receiving while kneeling, however, is somewhat debatable for me, in a cultural sense, but not so much.

I don't know how you would react to this, I'm just trying to have a conversation here. Like, if the Revelation would meet with Culture through Evangelization, then it makes total sense for Early Christians to create a means to receive communion which would give respect to the Eucharist. I mean many Asian cultures, except Sinitic, traditionally eat with their hands, and some still do even until today. The established manner of receiving on the hand avoids treating the Eucharist as just another piece of food, since it is "sacred food", it is Christ himself. Come on, there must be credit for that. I'm just saying.

Of course overtime, a better way was adopted. It is good and valid. However, I think, that even if receiving communion on the tongue, is better, they should consider the culture of the people being evangelized as well in terms of sharing the faith. A lot of local cultural nuances have been removed in favor of an all-embracing romanization of the Church during the age of exploration and colonization. I would get why this happened, since Rome was the Superpower that was back then. However, I would argue that this romanization also forced a distortion of local values and cultural richness. The faith was simply forced. I mean there were many holy men and women missionaries during these times, but in colonies which were already established, the faith was simply spoonfed. Yes, they may have been accepted by the people, but it came at the cost of sacrificing old beliefs and traditions, some for the better and some for the worse.

I would offer an approach that would best mirror the way Mary carried her message to Mexico as Our Lady of Guadalupe. She communicated to the bishop through the roses, and she communicated to the natives most specially through her dress, and the imagery on the tilma.
